I've been doing some debugging with Claude Opus 4.7 and determined that the permissions don't seem to work consistently.

For context, I found that while I have a lot of read bash commands allow-listed, I was still prompted for individual commands and chains of commands where each command in the chain is already allow-listed. The latter feels like a configuration option that should be included, but for now I decided to use Claude via OpenCode to write a new plugin that would do the right thing. I noticed while writing this plugin continual permission requests, which I've always had, and then I decided to test the plugin. I found the results inconsistent, so I asked Claude why. The result was a rabbit hole (it was kinda funny watching the investigation unfold), and this was the summary:

```
opencode's bash permission engine intermittently fails to apply configured
`permission.bash` allow rules. The same input string can evaluate to
different rules within the same session — and even within the same single
permission request that covers a chained command. The result is that the
agent is prompted to approve commands that should be silently allowed
based on the user's configuration.

The user's resolved (post-merge) bash ruleset clearly contains rules like
`"head *": "allow"`, `"cat *": "allow"`, `"pwd": "allow"`, etc., as
confirmed by `opencode debug config`. But the engine often evaluates
matching inputs to the hardcoded fallback `{permission: "*", pattern: "*",
action: "ask"}`, which is what `evaluate()` returns when no rule matches.
```
I've included files that represent the performed investigation and outcomes. I have replaced certain specific paths with `<REDACTED>` out of an abundance of caution to avoid leaking anything my company might not want to be out there, but I assure you they are valid and very 'normal' paths (no weird characters, no symlinks, no weird permissions set, etc.).

Because much of this seems to be inconsistent, I don't know how to do a repro step; I'm hoping the included logs and description will help debug the issue though. I'd suggest reading REPORT.md first to understand the context and then dig into the other files, if someone decides to make use of this info.

[opencode.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28482541/opencode.json)
[REPORT.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28482545/REPORT.md)
[resolved-permission.json](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28482543/resolved-permission.json)

Ok, found an edge case were for specific types of updates that landed after scrolling back to the bottom. Try https://github.com/anomalyco/opentui/pull/1141 and see if it corrects on your end. Tried it a few different ways here and it seems to have fixed the case.

Thanks for taking a look! A super quick test seems better. Let me kick the tires with it a bit over the next couple days to confirm.

@ualtinok Thanks for both the field data and the design instinct here. The ~38% reduction over 15 days lands right next to the ~41% my cache simulation estimated in #16848 (comment) (https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/issues/16848#issuecomment-4028637673), so two independent methods are converging on "this is a large pile of money."

Subagents are a clean discriminator. Ephemeral subagents rarely resume activity after a 5m gap because there's no human sitting and thinking, so they'd mostly just eat the 2.0x write premium with no payback. I dug into the code and the signal is already present at request-prep time (agent.mode === "subagent", and equivalently a non-null parentSessionID), so it's implementable without heuristics.

Where I'm still uncertain is the right long-term control surface for it: a static subagent-detection heuristic baked into defaults, the current env-var approach, a config knob, or some combination. That deserves its own discussion after we stop the bleeding rather than something to settle inline here.

My proposal: land this PR as-is. It's the conservative move: opt-in, defaults to the cheaper 5m, and matches Claude Code's per-token semantics. It only benefits users paying close enough attention to spot the env var, which is exactly the population that can evaluate the tradeoff for their workflow. That stops a major source of waste for power users today without changing anyone's defaults. Then, once it's merged, I'll open a follow-up issue on extending these benefits to a less-technical audience.

## Update: rebased and restructured to follow the LLMEvent pipeline

After reviewing the codebase architecture, the original approach of reading `value.response.headers` directly in `processor.ts` was bypassing the established data flow. This update restructures the change to follow the same pattern used by `providerMetadata`.

**What changed:**

- `packages/llm/src/schema/events.ts` — added `responseHeaders` to the `StepFinish` event schema (the correct entry point for data flowing from providers)
- `packages/opencode/src/session/llm/ai-sdk.ts` — captures `event.response?.headers` from the AI SDK `finish-step` event and passes it into the `stepFinish` LLM event
- `packages/opencode/src/session/message-v2.ts` — `responseHeaders` field on the `Assistant` schema unchanged in intent; also fixed a stray `.annotate()` call left by a bad merge
- `packages/opencode/src/session/processor.ts` — updated to read `value.responseHeaders` (from the LLM event) instead of `value.response.headers` (AI SDK raw)

**Verified:** `bun turbo typecheck` — all 19 packages pass. Built and smoke-tested locally.

After comparing #30085 and #30288, #30288 is clearly the better fix. It inherits parent session permissions cleanly, respects the existing allow/deny model, and follows least privilege—unlike #30085 which hard‑codes full MCP access. Go with #30288.

**Why this belongs in the ecosystem docs:**

I mined 227 real OpenCode sessions and classified agent stops using a 3-way Haiku majority vote (user's reply as ground truth). **78% were premature** — 91 permission-seeking ("Want me to run the tests?" when Bash is available), 68 stopped-with-todos (listed next steps and stopped).

The plugin fires on `session.idle`, classifies the stop, and re-prompts with targeted feedback when the agent quit early. Two detectors:
- **PLANNING_LOOP**: many tool calls, low write ratio → "stop reading, start writing"
- **ACTION_LOOP**: repeated identical commands → "try a different approach"

Enforces workflow gates: tests ran + passed, PR created, CI green.

Install: `{ "plugin": ["opencode-reflection"] }` in `opencode.json`

The Medium writeup with full methodology: https://medium.com/@dzianisv/vibe-engineering-reflection-a-completion-verification-layer-for-autonomous-ai-coding-agents-deb193d5a848

Re the bot's pointer to #28743 (wildcard CORS): the two are complementary, not overlapping.

- **#28743** adds a general, operator-configurable wildcard mechanism for the `--cors` allowlist — broad and powerful, but opt-in config that widens the configurable surface.
- **This PR** is a narrow, scheme-specific *default* allowance for `vscode-webview://`, mirroring the `tauri://localhost` allowance directly above it. Both are local IDE host schemes wrapping the same loopback API, with no real cross-origin boundary.

The distinction that matters is default behavior: VS Code assigns every WebviewPanel a fresh `vscode-webview://<random-guid>` origin, so without a built-in allowance an embedding extension must either restart the opencode process on every new panel to refresh an exact-match `--cors` entry (killing any in-flight turn), or lean on #28743's wildcard — which means every operator embedding opencode in an IDE has to know to configure it. Allowing the scheme by default (as we already do for tauri) makes IDE embedding work out of the box. Happy to consolidate if you'd prefer a single direction.

I created a sandbox that is not a container (which has its benefits): 

1. A sandbox based on Landlock LSM and SECCOMP (latter for a few corner cases e.g., `bind()`): https://github.com/jarkkojs/landstrip
2. A proof-of-concept integration: https://github.com/jarkkojs/pi-hashline-readmap

Landstrip appears more in semantics like Seatbelt than containers. It's also designed to be easy to nail in like e.g., not having dependecies to `/etc`, not requiring any special privileges, being enabled in the distribution and enterprise kernels etc.

I had had this idea for some time so I just decided to try how it works in practice. Seems to work pretty well :-) Just thought that this could potentially ease up the cross-platform sudoku.

I made also this table, which kind of makes apparent how Landstrip and Seatbelt meet quite nicely:

| Area         | Seatbelt                 | Landstrip                    |
| ------------ | ------------------------ | -----------------------------|
| Policy       | path based rules         | file based rules             |
| Timing       | dynamic subset of paths  | file based static ruleset    |
| TCP          | localhost proxy ports    | loopback proxy ports         |
| Unix sockets | allowlist                | allowlist via seccomp broker |

I.e. macOS is more dynamic and Linux is more secure because paths are ambiguous links to underlying inodes :-) (path based access control is always prone to middleman attacks).
